concept.name: Intrinsic value
concept.definition: The value an option would have if exercised immediately: the amount by which the underlying price exceeds the strike for a call, or by which the strike exceeds the underlying price for a put; only in-the-money options have intrinsic value.
concept.intuition: Intrinsic value is the cash you could capture right now by exercising and trading out of the underlying — everything above that in the premium is hope, not substance.
concept.mechanics: For a call with underlying price S and strike K, intrinsic value = max(S - K, 0); for a put, max(K - S, 0). It sets a lower bound on an American-style option's premium, since selling the option for less than intrinsic value would invite immediate-exercise arbitrage.
concept.formula: Call: IV = max(S - K, 0); Put: IV = max(K - S, 0), where S = current underlying price and K = strike price.
concept.failure_modes: For deep-in-the-money or hard-to-borrow underlyings, quoted premiums can briefly deviate from intrinsic value when the underlying's price is stale or early exercise is optimal, so 'intrinsic value' computed from a stale quote misleads.
concept.misconceptions: Intrinsic value is not the same as profit: an in-the-money option still loses money for its buyer if the premium paid exceeds the intrinsic value realized.
concept.example: With the underlying stock at $32.80, a $32.50-strike call has $0.30 of intrinsic value; if its premium is $1.10, the remaining $0.80 is time value.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
The Options Industry Council (OIC): Options Pricing
